book.title: Thinking in Systems
book.author: Donella H. Meadows
book.sourceLabel: WeRead table of contents and community highlights; English synthesis and paraphrase

thesis.hook: Stop reacting to events. Redesign the structure that keeps producing them.
thesis.statement: A system's behavior emerges from its stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays, rules, goals, and underlying paradigms. Durable change begins by seeing those relationships as a whole.

quoteChain.label: Events
quoteChain.text: A single event tells you what happened, but not why it keeps happening.

quoteChain.label: Patterns
quoteChain.text: Connect events across time and recurring behavior becomes visible.

quoteChain.label: Structure
quoteChain.text: Recurring behavior is the fingerprint of stocks, loops, delays, rules, and goals.

quoteChain.label: Nonlinearity
quoteChain.text: In a nonlinear world, linear intuition is an unreliable guide.

quoteChain.label: Leverage
quoteChain.text: Changing numbers is easy; changing information, rules, goals, and paradigms reaches deeper.

quoteChain.label: Practice
quoteChain.text: Systems cannot be fully controlled, but they can be observed, redesigned, and learned with.

branches.label: System Anatomy
branches.summary: A system is not merely a collection of things. It is a set of elements connected in ways that produce behavior toward a purpose.

notes.title: Elements
notes.body: People, machines, resources, and institutions are visible, but replacing them often leaves the system's behavior largely intact.

notes.title: Interconnections
notes.body: Information, incentives, material flows, and causal relationships determine how elements influence one another.

notes.title: Purpose
notes.body: The real goal is inferred from persistent behavior—what the system repeatedly rewards, protects, or sacrifices—not from stated intentions.

notes.title: Boundary
notes.body: No system is truly isolated. Choose a boundary that is wide enough to explain the behavior relevant to your question.

branches.question: If every visible element were replaced but the connections and purpose remained, what behavior would persist?

branches.label: Stocks & Flows
branches.summary: Stocks are the memory of a system. Flows change them over time, while the size of the stock creates inertia, buffering, and delay.

notes.title: Stock
notes.body: An accumulation such as cash, population, trust, inventory, skill, or atmospheric carbon records the system's present condition.

notes.title: Inflow
notes.body: Anything entering the stock increases it: hiring, deposits, learning, births, production, or replenishment.

notes.title: Outflow
notes.body: Anything leaving the stock decreases it: attrition, spending, forgetting, deaths, sales, or depletion.

notes.title: Dynamic equilibrium
notes.body: A stock can remain constant while large flows pass through it, provided inflow and outflow are equal.

branches.question: For the problem you care about, what is accumulating, and which flow is easiest to change sustainably?

branches.label: Feedback Loops
branches.chapter: Part I and Chapter 2 — The System Zoo
branches.summary: Feedback makes causality circular: results return as information that changes future action. System behavior usually comes from several loops competing at once.

notes.title: Reinforcing loop
notes.body: A change produces more change in the same direction—growth, decline, compounding, contagion, or escalation.

notes.title: Balancing loop
notes.body: The system compares its current state with a goal and acts to close the gap, producing regulation or oscillation.

notes.title: Dominance shift
notes.body: Different loops dominate at different times; early growth may later be constrained by resource limits.

notes.title: Loop literacy
notes.body: Read a loop as a story through time: if this rises, what changes next, and how does that eventually return to the starting variable?

branches.question: Which reinforcing loop drives the behavior, and which balancing loop is trying to contain it?

branches.label: Delay & Surprise
branches.chapter: Part II and Chapter 4 — Why Systems Surprise Us
branches.summary: Systems surprise us because feedback arrives late, relationships are nonlinear, boundaries are selective, and each actor sees only a limited part of the whole.

notes.title: Delay
notes.body: When results arrive long after action, people keep correcting an outdated state and create overshoot, oscillation, or collapse.

notes.title: Nonlinearity
notes.body: The same action can have different effects at different states, because relationships bend, saturate, and encounter thresholds.

notes.title: Limiting factor
notes.body: Growth is constrained by whichever necessary resource is relatively most scarce; after one limit is removed, another often becomes binding.

notes.title: Bounded rationality
notes.body: Actors make locally sensible choices using incomplete information and incentives, yet their combined actions can damage the whole.

branches.question: What delayed consequence or invisible limit could reverse today's apparently successful trend?

branches.label: Traps & Resistance
branches.summary: Recurring failures are often archetypal structures. Naming the trap reveals why familiar fixes backfire and where a countermeasure belongs.

notes.title: Policy resistance
notes.body: Actors pursue conflicting goals; each intervention triggers compensating behavior elsewhere. Align them under a larger shared goal.

notes.title: Drift to low performance
notes.body: Poor results lower expectations, which reduces corrective effort and normalizes decline. Anchor standards to the best achieved level.

notes.title: Shifting the burden
notes.body: A quick external fix relieves symptoms while weakening the system's ability to solve the cause. Restore internal capacity and withdraw dependency carefully.

notes.title: Wrong goal
notes.body: A proxy metric replaces the real purpose, so the system optimizes what is countable rather than what matters. Redesign the measure around total welfare.
notes.cue: What is the metric actually rewarding?

branches.question: Which recurring failure becomes predictable once you name its feedback structure?

branches.label: Leverage & Practice
branches.chapter: Part III and Chapter 7 — Living in a World of Systems
branches.summary: Leverage increases as intervention moves from quantities toward information, rules, goals, paradigms, and the capacity to transcend paradigms—but resistance usually increases too.

notes.title: Low leverage
notes.body: Changing constants, buffers, physical structures, or delays may help, but often leaves the system's reason for behaving untouched.
notes.cue: Am I only changing a number?

notes.title: Structural leverage
notes.body: Strengthening feedback, restoring information, changing rules, and enabling self-organization reshape how the system adapts.

notes.title: Intent leverage
notes.body: Changing goals and paradigms changes what the system considers success and therefore reorganizes many lower-level choices at once.

notes.title: Dance, do not dominate
notes.body: Observe before intervening, test small moves, monitor feedback, remain humble, and change course as the system reveals itself.
notes.cue: What did the system just teach me?

branches.question: What is the highest leverage intervention you can make without pretending to know more than you do?

systemProperties.name: Resilience
systemProperties.definition: The ability to absorb disturbance and restore function through multiple balancing pathways, redundancy, and diversity.
systemProperties.risk: Short-term efficiency programs often remove the spare capacity that resilience needs.

systemProperties.name: Self-organization
systemProperties.definition: The ability to create new structures, rules, and behaviors from within—learning, adaptation, evolution, and innovation.
systemProperties.risk: Rigid control can suppress experimentation and make a system brittle.

systemProperties.name: Hierarchy
systemProperties.definition: Nested subsystems reduce information burden and allow complex systems to evolve from stable intermediate forms.
systemProperties.risk: Higher levels fail when they dominate rather than serve the functioning of lower levels.

surprises.name: Event fixation
surprises.explanation: We react to headlines and incidents instead of tracking behavior over time.
surprises.practice: Graph the variable across a meaningful time horizon.

surprises.name: Linear intuition
surprises.explanation: We expect proportional cause and effect in systems shaped by thresholds and saturation.
surprises.practice: Look for curves, capacity limits, and tipping points.

surprises.name: Narrow boundaries
surprises.explanation: We define the system too tightly and export consequences beyond what we chose to see.
surprises.practice: Redraw the boundary around the decision's real purpose.

surprises.name: Layers of limits
surprises.explanation: Removing one constraint reveals another, so growth rarely remains unconstrained.
surprises.practice: Ask which factor becomes limiting next.

surprises.name: Ubiquitous delays
surprises.explanation: Causes and effects are separated in time, hiding responsibility and inviting overcorrection.
surprises.practice: Estimate the delay before changing course again.

surprises.name: Bounded rationality
surprises.explanation: Local information and incentives make individually rational behavior collectively destructive.
surprises.practice: Improve visibility and align local goals with the whole.

traps.name: Policy resistance
traps.pattern: Several actors pull the stock toward incompatible goals.
traps.countermove: Stop overpowering resistance; align around a larger shared objective.

traps.name: Tragedy of the commons
traps.pattern: Individuals receive benefits while costs are distributed across a shared resource.
traps.countermove: Restore feedback, regulate access, educate users, or privatize with safeguards.

traps.name: Drift to low performance
traps.pattern: Bad performance lowers the reference standard, reducing corrective action.
traps.countermove: Keep an absolute standard and compare with the best historical performance.

traps.name: Escalation
traps.pattern: One actor's gain threatens another, triggering a reinforcing contest.
traps.symptom: Arms races, price wars, status competition.
traps.countermove: Refuse the contest or negotiate a balancing structure and shared limit.

traps.name: Success to the successful
traps.pattern: Early winners receive more resources, which makes them more likely to win again.
traps.countermove: Diversify rewards, level the field, or constrain the winning loop.

traps.name: Shifting the burden
traps.pattern: A fast symptomatic fix weakens the slower fundamental solution.
traps.countermove: Strengthen internal capacity and withdraw the quick fix gradually.

traps.name: Rule beating
traps.pattern: Actors obey the letter of a rule while defeating its purpose.
traps.symptom: Targets are met but outcomes deteriorate.
traps.countermove: Redesign rules to reflect the true purpose and reduce exploitability.

traps.name: Seeking the wrong goal
traps.pattern: A measurable proxy replaces the system's actual welfare.
traps.symptom: The metric improves while reality worsens.
traps.countermove: Specify the real outcome and measure it directly where possible.

leveragePoints.name: Constants and parameters
leveragePoints.idea: Taxes, subsidies, standards, and numerical settings are visible but usually leave structure intact.

leveragePoints.name: Buffer sizes
leveragePoints.idea: Larger stocks can stabilize a system, but oversized buffers may create rigidity or cost.

leveragePoints.name: Stock-and-flow structure
leveragePoints.idea: Physical and organizational architecture sets what movement is possible, though rebuilding is expensive.

leveragePoints.name: Delays
leveragePoints.idea: Shorten information delays or slow the system so action and feedback can stay aligned.

leveragePoints.name: Balancing-loop strength
leveragePoints.idea: Improve the system's capacity to detect deviation and restore its desired state.

leveragePoints.name: Reinforcing-loop gain
leveragePoints.idea: Slow harmful compounding before trying to overpower it with balancing controls.

leveragePoints.name: Information flows
leveragePoints.idea: Put missing information where decisions are made; visibility can alter behavior without coercion.

leveragePoints.name: Rules
leveragePoints.idea: Incentives, punishments, permissions, and constraints define the game people optimize.

leveragePoints.name: Self-organization
leveragePoints.idea: Enable the system to learn, diversify, evolve, and create new structures.

leveragePoints.name: Goals
leveragePoints.idea: Change what the system is trying to accomplish and lower-level behavior reorganizes around it.

leveragePoints.name: Paradigms
leveragePoints.idea: Change the shared assumptions from which goals, rules, and measurements arise.

leveragePoints.name: Transcending paradigms
leveragePoints.idea: Hold every worldview lightly enough to notice its limits and choose among frames.

practices: Get the beat of the system before trying to change it.
Bring your mental models into the open and invite challenge.
Honor, release, and distribute information accurately.
Use language carefully and expand it to describe complexity.
Attend to what matters, not only to what is easy to measure.
Design feedback policies that adapt as the system changes.
Choose the good of the whole over the optimization of one part.
Listen for the system's existing wisdom before replacing it.
Place responsibility where decisions and consequences meet.
Stay humble, experiment, monitor, and remain a learner.
Celebrate complexity instead of demanding one-cause explanations.
Expand the time horizon far enough to see delayed effects.
Cross disciplinary boundaries; systems do not respect departments.
Expand the boundary of care to include distant people and futures.
Do not erode the goal of goodness when reality falls short.

toolkit.name: Name the behavior
toolkit.prompt: What keeps happening—not just what happened today?

toolkit.name: Choose the stock
toolkit.prompt: What quantity or quality is accumulating or depleting?

toolkit.name: Draw the flows
toolkit.prompt: What raises or lowers that stock over time?

toolkit.name: Close the loops
toolkit.prompt: How does the result return to influence future action?

toolkit.name: Mark delays and limits
toolkit.prompt: Where is feedback late, nonlinear, or constrained?

toolkit.name: Test the goal
toolkit.prompt: What does persistent behavior reveal about the real objective?

toolkit.name: Search upward for leverage
toolkit.prompt: Can information, rules, goals, or paradigms change the pattern?

toolkit.name: Run a small experiment
toolkit.prompt: What reversible move would produce useful feedback quickly?

glossary.meaning: Interconnected elements organized to achieve a function or purpose.
A quantity or quality accumulated over time; the memory of the system.
A rate that increases or decreases a stock.
A closed causal chain in which a change eventually influences itself.
A loop that amplifies change in the same direction.
A loop that acts to reduce the gap between a state and a goal.
Time between action, consequence, measurement, or response.
A relationship whose effect changes with system state or scale.
Capacity to absorb disruption and recover function.
Capacity to create new structure and behavior from within.
A place where a small shift can produce a large behavioral change.
A shared worldview from which a system's goals, rules, and measures arise.

comparison.title: Event Reaction vs. Systems Intervention
comparison.conclusion: A systems intervention may look slower at first, but it changes the conditions that reproduce the problem.

memoryPrompts.question: What three components define a system?
memoryPrompts.answer: Elements, interconnections, and a function or purpose.

memoryPrompts.question: Why can replacing every visible element leave behavior unchanged?
memoryPrompts.answer: Because the interconnections and purpose that generate behavior may remain intact.

memoryPrompts.question: How do stocks create both stability and delay?
memoryPrompts.answer: They buffer short-term changes, but their accumulated mass takes sustained flow to alter.

memoryPrompts.question: What is the difference between reinforcing and balancing feedback?
memoryPrompts.answer: Reinforcing loops amplify change; balancing loops act to close a gap against a target.

memoryPrompts.question: Why do delays cause overshoot?
memoryPrompts.answer: Actors continue correcting before previous actions become visible, so total intervention exceeds what was needed.

memoryPrompts.question: Name the three capacities that help systems work well.
Which trap turns a quick fix into long-term dependence?
memoryPrompts.answer: Shifting the burden to the intervener.

memoryPrompts.question: Which trap makes a metric improve while the real outcome worsens?
Why are information flows often a high-leverage intervention?
memoryPrompts.answer: They change decisions at the point of action without necessarily rebuilding physical structure.

memoryPrompts.question: What lies above rules in the leverage hierarchy?
memoryPrompts.answer: Self-organization, goals, paradigms, and the ability to transcend paradigms.

memoryPrompts.question: What does it mean to dance with a system?
memoryPrompts.answer: Observe, experiment, monitor feedback, stay humble, and revise rather than trying to command a complex future.

memoryPrompts.question: Apply the method to one recurring problem: what is the stock, the loop, the delay, and the real goal?
memoryPrompts.answer: A good answer names an accumulation, traces at least one closed causal loop, marks delayed feedback, and distinguishes stated from revealed goals.
